c.tagline: Ancient Roman ruins meet buzzing hillside cafes in the Levant's white city.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are required by law; insist drivers use them, as fixed/negotiated fares are common from the airport and near tourist sites.

emergency.note: Tourist Police can be reached at 121; Civil Defense (fire/ambulance) also responds via 911 in most areas.

avoid.reason: Very safe; usual petty-crime caution; avoid demonstrations

hood_desc: Historic hillside core packed with the Roman Theatre, gold souks and cheap eateries; best for budget travelers and culture-seekers who want to be steps from the old city's chaos and charm.

Amman's most walkable, hip hillside quarter along Rainbow Street with boutique cafes, art galleries and nightlife; suits first-time visitors and younger travelers wanting atmosphere close to downtown.
A central business and hotel district with wide boulevards, malls and international chain hotels; suits business travelers and anyone wanting a convenient, modern base near West Amman.
Leafy, upscale residential district with embassies, fine dining and Amman's trendiest bars; suits travelers wanting comfort, security and a Western-style night out.
Amman's newest downtown, built around a glossy modern boulevard with towers, shopping and 5-star hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting brand-new infrastructure near transit hubs.

water.note: Municipally treated and generally safe, but rooftop storage tanks can affect quality, so bottled water is a safer bet for visitors.

transit.pay: Cash paid on board for most local buses and service taxis (small flat fares in fils/JD); JETT intercity tickets are bought at counters or online. There is no rechargeable transit card system in wide use as of 2026.
transit.hours: Public buses generally run roughly 6:00-20:00; service taxis and private taxis operate much later, effectively covering nights.
transit.note: Amman has no metro or tram; most visitors rely on taxis/rideshare (Careem, Uber) plus walking within neighborhoods, since the bus network is not clearly signed for tourists.

train: Hejaz Jordan Railway (limited heritage/cargo service, no regular passenger timetable)
bus: Public Transport Regulatory Commission city buses

transit.m: Airport Express bus to Amman (Tabarbour/7th Circle), 45-60 min

tip.r: About 10% is appreciated in restaurants (some already add a service charge); round up taxi fares and tip hotel staff a dinar or two.

food.name: Mansaf
food.desc: Jordan's national dish: lamb simmered in tangy fermented jameed yoghurt over rice and shrak bread, eaten from a shared platter.

places.name: Reem Al Bawadi
places.note: Vast terraced dining hall where Jordanian families come for occasion mansaf.

places.name: Tawaheen Al Hawa
places.note: Good lamb, proper jameed and portions sized for two rather than twelve.

food.name: Knafeh Nabulsieh
food.desc: Molten white cheese under orange shredded pastry, drowned in sugar syrup and pistachios, cut by the kilo and eaten standing up.

places.name: Habibah Sweets
places.note: The alley hole-in-the-wall branch is the one locals queue at; cash, no seats.

places.name: Nafeeseh Sweets
places.note: Long-running rival for the city's best knafeh; also excellent baklava.

food.name: Falafel
food.desc: Herb-green chickpea fritters fried to order and wrapped in bread with tahini and pickles; breakfast for half of Amman.

places.name: Hashem Restaurant
places.note: Open since the 1950s in an alley off King Faisal Street; falafel, foul and tea only.

places.name: Al Quds Falafel
places.note: Since 1966; the sesame kaak sandwich with tahini is the order to make.

food.name: Shawarma
food.desc: Thin-shaved spit-roasted lamb or chicken rolled tight in flatbread with tahini or garlic sauce and pickles, grilled crisp on the press.

places.name: Shawerma Reem
places.note: Family-run street window running three decades; expect a pavement queue after dark.

places.name: Shawerma 3a Saj
places.note: Amman-style wraps with punchy garlic sauce or beef with pomegranate molasses.

food.name: Maqluba
food.desc: The upside-down pot: rice layered with fried aubergine, cauliflower and chicken or lamb, flipped onto a tray at the table.

places.name: Sufra
places.note: Old villa with a garden terrace; the most atmospheric Jordanian home cooking in town.

places.name: Beit Sitti
places.note: Cook maqluba yourself with local grandmothers, then eat it on the terrace.

food.name: Musakhan
food.desc: Levantine roast chicken heavy with sumac and slow-caramelised onion, served on olive-oil-soaked taboon bread with toasted pine nuts.

places.name: Sufra
places.note: Reliable, well-spiced version alongside mezze and fresh bread from the clay oven.

places.name: Fakhr El-Din
places.note: Elegant 1950s villa; the polished, special-occasion take on Levantine classics.

food.name: Limonana
food.desc: Fresh lemon blitzed with mint and ice into a slushy, sharp green cooler; the default order on every Amman terrace in summer.

places.name: Sufra
places.note: Made to order on the garden terrace, unsweetened if you ask.

places.name: Rainbow Street juice bars
places.note: Cheap street windows squeezing lemon-mint and fresh fruit juices until late.

food.name: Arabic coffee and sage tea
food.desc: Cardamom-heavy qahwa sada in tiny cups, or Bedouin shai with sage or mint poured sweet; both are hospitality, not a caffeine fix.

places.name: Jafra Cafe
places.note: First-floor cafe above the old street; coffee, tea and live oud most evenings.

places.name: Rakwet Arab
places.note: Retro Jordanian cafe built for slow tea, backgammon and cardamom coffee.

landmarks: Amman Citadel (Jabal al-Qal'a)
A hilltop archaeological site with Roman, Byzantine, and Umayyad ruins offering the best panoramic views over Amman's seven hills.
Roman Theatre of Amman
A massive, beautifully preserved 2nd-century Roman amphitheater carved into a hillside, still used for performances today.
King Abdullah I Mosque
Amman's most recognizable mosque, crowned by a huge blue mosaic dome that dominates the city's skyline.
Temple of Hercules
The towering Roman columns of this ancient temple atop the Citadel are among Amman's most photographed ruins.
Rainbow Street
A trendy, historic street lined with cafes, art galleries, and Ottoman-era buildings, perfect for soaking up local life.
The Nymphaeum of Amman
An elaborate 2nd-century Roman public fountain, one of the largest of its kind in the ancient world.
Al-Husseini Mosque
A landmark pink-and-white mosque in downtown Amman built on the site of an ancient structure, at the heart of the bustling old souk district.
Jordan Museum
The country's leading museum, home to treasures including the Dead Sea Scrolls fragments and the Ain Ghazal statues.
Odeon of Amman
A smaller, elegantly preserved Roman theater near the Nymphaeum, notable for its intimate scale and intricate stonework.
Duke's Diwan (Beit Sakakini)
One of downtown Amman's oldest buildings, a beautifully restored heritage house symbolizing the city's early 20th-century architecture.

train.note: Jordan has no scheduled passenger rail. The historic Hejaz Jordan Railway from Amman runs only occasional tourist/charter trips, and the Damascus–Amman line has been suspended since 2006. Travel between cities is by bus or road.

bus.note: JETT is Jordan's main long-distance coach operator, with a scheduled Amman–Cairo service (~20h, via the Aqaba/Nuweiba crossing). Crossings to Israel and the West Bank (King Hussein/Allenby and Sheikh Hussein bridges) are usually done by shared taxi/JETT shuttle rather than a through coach; the Amman–Damascus route remains suspended. Bring your passport and check border status.

ferry.note: Amman is inland with no port. The nearest sea crossing is the Aqaba–Nuweiba (Egypt) fast/car ferry, about 4h south of Amman, operated by AB Maritime. HUMAN EDITOR: verify AB Maritime's current official booking URL before publishing.

half.name: Jerash
half.blurb: One of the world's best-preserved Roman provincial cities, with colonnaded streets, temples and theatres.

half.name: Dead Sea
half.blurb: Earth's lowest point, where salty mineral waters let you float effortlessly and coat in mud.

half.name: Madaba
half.blurb: The City of Mosaics, famous for its ancient Byzantine map of the Holy Land.

half.name: Mount Nebo
half.blurb: The hilltop where Moses reputedly viewed the Promised Land, with sweeping valley panoramas.

half.name: Bethany Beyond the Jordan
half.blurb: The riverside baptism site of Jesus, an atmospheric pilgrimage spot beside the Jordan River.

full.name: Petra
full.blurb: The rose-red Nabataean city carved into sandstone cliffs, reached through the dramatic narrow Siq.
